title: Feasibility of Distributed Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing: From Quantum Links to Algorithms
authors: Takumi Kobayashi, Hodaka Kurokawa, Yasunari Suzuki, Hideo Kosaka
abstract: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a large number of physical qubits, posing a major challenge for scaling up individual quantum processors. Distributed architectures offer a promising solution by interconnecting multiple processors through quantum networks. However, remote Bell-pair generation remains technically demanding, making it essential to assess computational performance under limited communication resources. In this work, we present a comprehensive resource analysis of distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation using superconducting processors connected by microwave or optical links. We show that even a single physical communication channel per node can substantially reduce the physical-qubit requirements per node under experimentally motivated, forward-looking microwave-link assumptions of a 1 MHz physical Bell-pair generation rate and 90% fidelity, although at the cost of a roughly tenfold increase in execution time. Conversely, reducing the execution-time overhead requires substantially greater communication resources, including higher Bell-pair fidelities and extensive multiplexing. These results demonstrate the potential feasibility of distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation with limited communication resources and provide a quantitative basis for balancing quantum-link performance, processor size, and execution time.
summary: This paper analyzes the resource overheads for building fault-tolerant quantum computers using distributed architectures connected by quantum links. By performing a detailed resource analysis, the authors show that while limited communication resources can drastically cut down on local qubit requirements, this improvement necessitates a significant slowdown in computation time. It offers a quantitative framework for balancing hardware link performance against computational speed.
main_problem: Assessing the feasibility and resource requirements for building large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers by connecting multiple smaller processors via quantum networks.
main_result: Distributed architectures can significantly reduce the required physical qubits per node using limited communication links, but this comes at the expense of a substantial increase in overall execution time.
method: The work employs a comprehensive, multi-stage resource analysis that tracks physical and logical Bell-pair generation, distillation, and consumption rates across the entire computation workflow.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a distributed quantum network comprising superconducting processors (nodes) interconnected by quantum links (microwave or optical). The analysis follows a sequence from physical Bell-pair generation to final algorithm execution.
key_observables: Physical and logical Bell-pair generation/distillation rates ($r_{	ext{Bell}}$), fidelities ($F_{	ext{Bell}}$), and the resulting space, time, and communication overheads.
important_parameters: Link parameters such as a 1 MHz physical Bell-pair generation rate and 90% fidelity are used in forward-looking assumptions; target logical fidelity is often set to $10^{-12}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis simplifies the case by focusing on logical Bell-pair consumption (teleportation) rather than direct remote two-qubit logical operations, and relies on specific, forward-looking hardware performance estimates.
figures_summary: Figure 1(b) details the five-step resource estimation procedure, from physical Bell-pair generation through to algorithm execution. Figure 2 outlines the full workflow, detailing steps from physical link generation to final resource estimation.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structured resource analysis: first, calculating physical Bell-pair generation (Step I); second, performing physical distillation (Step II); third, generating logical Bell-pairs (Step III); fourth, performing logical distillation (Step IV); and finally, estimating the overall resource overhead for the quantum algorithm (Step V).
why_interesting: This work provides crucial quantitative metrics for scaling quantum computation, directly addressing the engineering bottleneck of connecting many smaller, imperfect quantum modules into a functional, large-scale machine.
